identity.title: Stability, Poles & Bode Plots
identity.tagline: Predicting whether a system will settle down, oscillate, or blow up — before it ever runs on real hardware.

simpleSummary: A set of tools for predicting, using math alone, whether a controlled system will calm down to its target or spiral out of control — critical to check before trusting a controller on real hardware like a drone.
keyIdea: A linear system's long-term behavior is completely determined by the locations of its transfer function's poles; poles in the stable region mean the system settles down, poles outside it mean the system oscillates or diverges.
overview: Once a system is expressed as a transfer function, its denominator — set equal to zero — is called the characteristic equation, and its roots are the system's poles. Poles are not just abstract math: each one corresponds to a natural mode of the system's response over time, and their locations in the complex plane completely determine whether that response decays toward zero (stable), stays at a constant oscillation (marginally stable), or grows without bound (unstable). Bode plots offer a complementary, frequency-domain view: they show how a system's output magnitude and phase shift respond across a whole range of input frequencies, which is especially useful for predicting how a real closed-loop (feedback) system behaves, including how close it is to instability under real-world imperfections like sensor noise or communication delay.

equations.label: Characteristic Equation
equations.meaning: Setting a transfer function's denominator to zero and solving for s gives the system's poles — the values of s where the transfer function becomes infinite.

equations.label: Stability Criterion
equations.meaning: A linear system is stable if and only if every pole has a negative real part — meaning every pole sits in the left half of the complex s-plane. Any pole with a positive real part means the response grows without bound.

howItWorks: A pole that is a negative real number corresponds to a response that decays smoothly like a simple exponential; a pair of complex poles with a negative real part corresponds to a decaying oscillation (ringing that dies out); a pole with a positive real part corresponds to a response that grows without bound — true instability. A pole sitting exactly on the imaginary axis (zero real part) is marginally stable: it neither grows nor decays, oscillating forever at a constant amplitude, which in practice is just as unusable as instability because any real disturbance pushes it one way or the other. Bode plots take a different angle: they plot a system's gain (in decibels) and phase shift as a function of input frequency, on logarithmic axes. For a closed-loop feedback system, the gain margin and phase margin read directly off a Bode plot indicate how much extra gain or delay the real system could tolerate before crossing into instability — a critical safety check, since simulations rarely capture every real-world imperfection (sensor lag, unmodeled friction, communication delay) that a physical system will actually experience. This is why control engineers check pole locations and stability margins analytically before ever deploying a controller onto hardware that could be damaged or dangerous if it becomes unstable.
diagramCaption: Left: the s-plane, where every pole in the shaded left half means a stable, decaying response, and any pole crossing into the right half means instability. Right: a simplified Bode magnitude plot, showing how gain rolls off with frequency.
realWorldExamples: Checking that a drone's flight controller has all closed-loop poles in the stable left-half plane before a single test flight — an unstable closed loop can crash a drone in well under a second.
Diagnosing a PID-controlled robot arm that oscillates persistently by reading its Bode plot's phase margin, revealing that the derivative gain needs increasing to add damping.
Comparing gain margin between a simulated controller and the same controller on real hardware, to account for real-world delays a simulation didn't model.
commonMisconceptions: "If it doesn't crash in a short simulation, it's stable" — marginal stability and slow-growing instabilities can look fine for a few seconds before clearly diverging.

"A system that's stable open-loop stays stable once you add feedback" — feedback (especially with high gain) can destabilize an otherwise perfectly stable system; this is exactly why stability analysis is done on the closed-loop system, not just the plant alone.

"Bode plots and pole locations are two completely different tools" — they describe the same underlying stability information from two different, mathematically connected viewpoints (frequency domain vs. complex-plane pole locations).
